Imaginary displacements and microhyperbolic cones

Written by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

A reciprocal may have a distributional boundary even at a multiple real zero. The useful hypothesis is that one imaginary displacement avoids every nearby zero. We prove that this hypothesis determines a convex cone from the first nonzero Taylor polynomial, gives a uniform reciprocal estimate inside smaller cones, and controls the analytic wavefront of the boundary inverse. The cone is optimal among closed convex bounds, although the actual wavefront fiber need not be convex. A four-dimensional light-cone calculation shows the distinction exactly.

The existing fixed-contour zero count and power sums and preparation component, Lemmas A–B supply zeros with multiplicities and smooth parameter-dependent moments. The contour foundation, Sections 16.2, 16.5 and 16.6, supplies local factorization, Cauchy's theorem and the bounded maximum principle. Complex polynomial factorization follows from U042, Lemma 3.0, followed by finite polynomial division. No continuity of individual root labels is assumed.

For distributions we use U015, Theorem 2.1, Corollary 2.2 and Theorem 3.2: full-cone boundary limits, moving tests and zero-boundary uniqueness. The analytic dual-cone estimate is U075, Theorem 2; the converse wedge construction is U081, Theorem 3 and Corollary 5. Closedness, conicity and the analytic singular-support projection are proved in U074. The spectral support estimate used in the final example is U082, Theorem 1. Finite-dimensional calculus, compactness, integration and Fourier normalization are supplied by the scalar, integration, angular and Fourier foundations.
